newsitem.title: USA: A much smaller Florida Medicaid case will be first.
newsitem.headline: A much smaller Florida Medicaid case will be first.

text.p: Mississippi's settlement with the tobacco industry Thursday has made Florida's Medicaid lawsuit against cigarette companies the first state case set for trial.
But the case scheduled to start next month is a shadow of the one filed two years ago.

In February 1995, Florida sued the tobacco industry, seeking $1.4 billion in reimbursement of taxpayer funds used to pay smoking-related public health costs. The Florida law under which the lawsuit was filed allowed the state to seek triple damages.
Florida also said it wanted some $16 billion from Big Tobacco to cover future costs and would ask for unspecified punitive damages going back decades.

In the months since, the lawsuit has been whittled down, most significantly this week when Palm Beach County Judge Harold Cohen barred the $16 billion future damages claim, although he told the state it was free to return to court repeatedly in later years to seek such reimbursement.

Last September, Cohen stripped all but three counts from the original 18-count lawsuit, including barring Florida from seeking reimbursement for Medicaid payments made before passage of its 1994 Medicaid Third-Party Liability Act, the law under which it filed the lawsuit.

"What Cohen has done is left us with a case which we can try and win," said Murray Garnick, a lawyer for leading cigarette maker Philip Morris, after several of Cohen's rulings this week. "It is far different from the one Florida presented."

Cohen also has freed the public relations firm Hill & Knowlton and two tobacco trade groups from liability in the lawsuit, cleared three holding companies -- Loews Corp, B.A.T Industries and BATUS Holdings Inc. -- and limited the state to seeking punitive damages dating back to 1982.
Florida's case is set to go to court before Judge Cohen on Aug. 4.
"I think he's slimmed it down, slimmed it, trimmed it," said Richard Daynard, head of the Tobacco Products Liability Project at Northeastern University.
But he said the judge has not gutted Florida's lawsuit. "(He has) in a sense cut out the stuff that he had doubts about but left the core of the state's case intact," Daynard said.

Florida is still seeking about $1 billion in actual damages, which can be tripled, plus unspecified punitive damages. Mississippi, which was to have gone to trial next week, settled its Medicaid lawsuit against tobacco companies for more than $3 billion over 25 years.
Legal experts also said they thought Florida's case was boosted because its claims are backed up by the 1994 statute.

"Florida was the state that specifically authorises recovery for that sort of thing," said Christopher Mueller, a University of Colorado law professor who teaches complex litigation. "... That definitely makes the chance of recovery and prevailing much higher."
Florida officials said Mississippi's settlement would not affect the state's pursuit of Big Tobacco.

"We spent a couple of hours across the table last week and came to the conclusion real, real quickly that there was just no way that Florida could settle at this point in time," Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth said. "We're just too far off."
